1. Introduction  
  • Definition and clinical role of sedative-hypnotics  
  • General mechanism: enhancement of inhibitory neurotransmission (predominantly GABAA)  

2. Barbiturates  
  A. Chemical properties  
    – Core: barbituric acid (pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione) scaffold  
    – Lipophilicity correlates with onset/duration (e.g. thiopental very lipophilic → ultrashort acting)  
    – pKa ~4 – 5; largely ionized at physiologic pH  
  B. Pharmacodynamics  
    – Positive allosteric modulation of GABAA; at higher concentrations direct channel opening  
    – Dose-dependent sedation → hypnosis → anesthesia → respiratory/CV depression  
  C. General synthetic strategy (conceptual)  
    – Condensation of diethyl/methyl malonate derivatives with urea → barbituric acid core  
    – C-5 alkylation/arylation introduces substituents that tune lipophilicity and kinetics  
  D. Therapeutic applications  
    – Historically insomnia, pre-anesthetic sedation; largely replaced by benzodiazepines  
    – Some (phenobarbital) still used in seizure disorders  
  E. Laboratory handling & safety  
    – Schedule III–IV controlled substances (depending on derivative)  
    – Use in fume hood, protective gloves/glasses; avoid inhalation of dust  
    – Waste: collect as controlled chemical waste per institutional guidelines  

3. Benzodiazepines  
  A. Chemical properties  
    – 1,4-Benzodiazepine core: fused benzene + seven-membered diazepine ring  
    – Substitutions at C-7 (electron-withdrawing for potency), N-1 and C-5 tune activity & half-life

  B. Pharmacodynamics  
    – Positive allosteric modulators of GABAA receptor → ↑ frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening

  C. General synthetic strategy (conceptual)  
    – Cyclocondensation of o-phenylenediamine with α-haloketones or ketoesters → 1,4-benzodiazepine scaffold  
    – Late-stage functionalization (e.g. N-alkylation, introduction of halogens or triazolo-rings)  
  D. Therapeutic applications  
    – Anxiety disorders, insomnia, muscle relaxation, seizure control, alcohol withdrawal  
  E. Laboratory handling & safety  
    – Controlled substance (Schedule IV in many jurisdictions)  
    – Protect from moisture; gloves, goggles, work in ventilated hood  
    – Keep accurate logs; secure storage  

4. “Z-Drugs” (Non-benzodiazepine GABAA modulators)  
  A. Examples: zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone  
  B. Chemical features: non-benzodiazepine scaffolds but bind benzodiazepine site on GABAA  
  C. Quick onset, short duration (insomnia treatment)

  E. Generally lower abuse potential but still controlled

  • Risk assessment: CNS depressants can cause respiratory depression, dependence, withdrawal  
  • Personal protective equipment: lab coat, gloves, eye protection, respirator if dusty/aerosols possible  
  • Engineering controls: fume hood or glovebox for powders  
  • Controlled-substance licensing: registration, secure storage, inventory management, record-keeping  
  • Waste disposal: collect unused/residue as hazardous and/or controlled waste; follow local regulations  

7. Summary of Therapeutic Profiles  
  • Barbiturates: broad spectrum but narrow therapeutic index; largely historical usage  
  • Benzodiazepines: versatile (anxiolytic, hypnotic, anticonvulsant) with relatively favorable safety profile  
  • Z-drugs: focused on insomnia with shorter durations, fewer next-day effects  
  • Other agents fill niches (allergic sedation, circadian disorders, neuropathic pain)
